item.title: As AI mass-produces historical dramas in China, where are the boundaries?
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: In 2026, AI is changing how historical dramas are produced in China. In the past, dramas featuring ancient battles, palace architecture and elaborate costumes often required large budgets and professional production teams. Today, AI generation and virtual compositing tools are making it possible for smaller teams and even individual creators to produce historical scenes that […]
item.content:encoded:
In 2026, AI is changing how historical dramas are produced in China. In the past, dramas featuring ancient battles, palace architecture and elaborate costumes often required large budgets and professional production teams.

Today, AI generation and virtual compositing tools are making it possible for smaller teams and even individual creators to produce historical scenes that were once difficult to realize. As production barriers fall, the volume of content is growing rapidly.

But as AI makes it possible to generate historical figures, battle scenes and depictions of ancient societies at scale, an important question emerges: when seemingly realistic historical narratives can be produced at low cost and in large quantities, how do we distinguish artistic interpretation from historical distortion?

The AI short drama boom raises questions about content quality

According to the 2026 H1 AI Drama and Animation Data Report released by industry research firm DataEye, China’s AI drama and animation market exceeded RMB 22 billion ($3.29 billion) in the first five months of 2026.

The market is projected to reach RMB 40 billion ($5.98 billion) for the full year, representing year-on-year growth of 138%. The audience base has also expanded rapidly, with the number of AI short-drama users in China surpassing 600 million in the first half of the year.

From January to June, 221,900 new AI short dramas were released, of which 1,055 surpassed 100 million views. These titles generated a combined 515.738 billion views. Monthly incremental views rose to 155.78 billion in June, the highest monthly figure in the first half of the year.

AI-generated historical content is also beginning to reach longer formats. The AI series Wielding Weapons in the Song Dynasty has reportedly maintained popularity scores above 46 million across multiple seasons.

Meanwhile, The Later Journey to the West, an AI-generated series, aired during Hunan Satellite TV’s prime-time slot, ranking first among provincial satellite channels in the same time slot during its broadcast.

For historical dramas, AI is lowering not only production costs but also the technical barriers to creating complex scenes. Ancient cities, palaces and large-scale battlefields can now be designed and composited with generative tools, giving smaller production teams more opportunities to explore historical storytelling.

However, an increase in output does not necessarily translate into better content. AI can generate convincing characters, costumes and architecture, but that does not mean these details are historically accurate. As images become increasingly realistic, audiences may find it easier to mistake visual authenticity for historical accuracy.

Historical dramas can take creative liberties, but fact and fiction should not be confused

Historical dramas are not the same as documentaries. Time travel, alternate histories and fictionalized retellings have long been part of screen storytelling. Artistic interpretation should not automatically be treated as a problem. The real question is how productions handle the boundary between historical fact and fiction.

AI introduces a new challenge because it can generate large amounts of detail in a short time. When information is incomplete, models may produce claims that sound plausible but lack historical evidence. Errors can involve people’s lives, clothing styles, the uses of artifacts and even the timelines of historical events.

A meticulously rendered ancient palace is not necessarily an accurate representation of architecture from that period. Likewise, a convincing dialogue attributed to a historical figure does not mean that the exchange is supported by historical records. If unverified details are presented as fact and repeated across large volumes of content, they may distort audiences’ understanding of history.

AI can therefore assist with historical research, scene design and image generation, but it cannot replace historical verification. For productions based on real historical events and figures, checking primary sources and consulting qualified experts remain essential.

How can content oversight protect both accuracy and creative freedom?

Rules governing short-form dramas are also evolving. The National Radio and Television Administration’s Measures for the Administration of Micro-Dramas, which took effect on September 1, 2026, introduced a classification-based management framework and set out requirements covering filing, review, distribution and disclosure labels for AI-generated content.

However, stronger content oversight does not mean that all AI historical dramas should face the same restrictions. Clearly identified alternate-history stories differ in their potential risks from productions based on real historical events that audiences may mistake for fact. The focus should not simply be on whether a work matches historical records in every detail, but also on whether it misleads audiences, violates applicable content rules or fails to meet reasonable standards of verification.

Platforms also need to look beyond views and engagement. As AI-generated content expands, stronger review processes, timely action against violations and appropriate disclosures about how content was produced will become increasingly important.

AI labels can tell audiences how a work was made, but they cannot replace fact-checking or exempt a production from other content requirements.

When generation becomes easy, what is the real barrier to entry?

AI historical dramas are giving more creators the opportunity to tell historical stories and bringing previously difficult creative ideas within reach. That is a meaningful change.

Yet as generating images becomes easier, the scarce skill may no longer be the ability to create an ancient palace, but knowing what that palace should have looked like in its historical context. It may no longer be the ability to generate a historical figure, but understanding that person’s era, background and documented experiences.

The challenge for AI historical dramas is therefore not simply how to increase production efficiency. It is how to balance artistic expression, historical accuracy and responsible distribution.

AI can certainly offer new ways to tell stories about the past, but the ability to generate a historical narrative does not justify disregarding historical facts. Technology can lower the barriers to creation, but creators’ understanding of history, their judgment about the boundaries of fiction, and platforms’ responsibility for the content they distribute will ultimately shape the results of this transformation.

item.title: XPENG names robotaxi service YOYO and opens invitation-based registration in China
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: XPENG announced XPENG YOYO as the brand for its robotaxi business on October 8 and opened online registration to users in China through invitation codes. The move expands access beyond employee testing as the company prepares for broader operations. The robotaxi uses four XPENG-developed Turing AI chips with a combined computing capacity of 3,000 TOPS […]
item.content:encoded:
XPENG announced XPENG YOYO as the brand for its robotaxi business on October 8 and opened online registration to users in China through invitation codes. The move expands access beyond employee testing as the company prepares for broader operations.

The robotaxi uses four XPENG-developed Turing AI chips with a combined computing capacity of 3,000 TOPS and runs the company’s VLA 2.0 model without lidar or high-definition maps. XPENG obtained permission in August to conduct road tests in Guangzhou without a safety operator in the driver’s seat, following production of its first robotaxi in May.

XPENG previously tested the booking and payment process internally at RMB 1 per ride. Chairman and CEO He Xiaopeng said the company plans to earn revenue through vehicle sales, services and commission sharing, with local fleet operations handled by partners. [XPENG]

item.title: LivSyn Robotics raises Series A funding for platform connecting robots with AI models
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Beijing-based LivSyn Robotics has secured a Series A round of at least RMB 100 million, according to an October 8 announcement. The round brought together financial investors, listed energy-services company Suwen Electric Energy and an undisclosed strategic investor in embodied AI. LivSyn develops RUDA, short for Robotics Unified Device Architecture, to connect different robot designs […]
item.content:encoded:
Beijing-based LivSyn Robotics has secured a Series A round of at least RMB 100 million, according to an October 8 announcement. The round brought together financial investors, listed energy-services company Suwen Electric Energy and an undisclosed strategic investor in embodied AI.

LivSyn develops RUDA, short for Robotics Unified Device Architecture, to connect different robot designs with AI models and agents. Its PhiAgent engine converts human demonstration videos into robot training data and motion trajectories, while RoboAgent handles task execution and feeds the results back into the system.

The company says its technology has been deployed in industrial applications including optical-module insertion and removal, battery assembly and electronics inspection. The platform is designed to let data and learned skills carry over between different robots, reducing the need to rebuild training and deployment systems for each new machine. [PEdaily, in Chinese]

item.title: Chinese brands to account for a third of automakers at Paris Motor Show
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: A record 20 Chinese car brands will participate in the 2026 Paris Motor Show, accounting for roughly a third of the approximately 60 automakers exhibiting at the event. The show opens on October 12, with Chinese participation doubling from 10 brands at the previous edition in 2024. BYD and Chery will be joined by newcomers […]
item.content:encoded:
A record 20 Chinese car brands will participate in the 2026 Paris Motor Show, accounting for roughly a third of the approximately 60 automakers exhibiting at the event. The show opens on October 12, with Chinese participation doubling from 10 brands at the previous edition in 2024.

BYD and Chery will be joined by newcomers including Aito and Avatr as Chinese manufacturers expand their European presence with electric and hybrid vehicles. Aito plans to present four premium electric SUVs for Europe and aims to increase overseas sales to 20% of its total within three years, up from less than 1% currently.

European manufacturers will also unveil new models as competition intensifies. François Roudier, secretary-general of the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers, said the arrival of Chinese brands had helped revive interest in motor shows as some traditional manufacturers reduced their participation. [Reuters]

item.title: AI glasses brand NIMO secures angel funding at RMB 1.5 billion valuation
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: The Chinese startup behind AI glasses brand NIMO has raised several hundred million yuan in angel funding, bringing its valuation to RMB 1.5 billion, according to an October 8 report. Investors include Gobi Partners, alongside other Chinese venture capital firms. The company develops smart glasses for everyday use and has established offline sales channels. It […]
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese startup behind AI glasses brand NIMO has raised several hundred million yuan in angel funding, bringing its valuation to RMB 1.5 billion, according to an October 8 report. Investors include Gobi Partners, alongside other Chinese venture capital firms.

The company develops smart glasses for everyday use and has established offline sales channels. It plans to use the proceeds to develop new products and core technologies, expand its domestic retail network and enter overseas markets, as more Chinese hardware startups compete in AI eyewear. [The Capital, in Chinese]

item.title: ByteDance merges TraeWork and TraeCode into unified TRAE platform
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: ByteDance has combined its office AI agent TraeWork and coding tool TraeCode into a unified TRAE platform, bringing task planning, content creation and software development into one application. Announced on October 9, the update lets users switch between Agent mode for managing tasks across projects and IDE mode for detailed coding and debugging. The platform […]
item.content:encoded:
ByteDance has combined its office AI agent TraeWork and coding tool TraeCode into a unified TRAE platform, bringing task planning, content creation and software development into one application. Announced on October 9, the update lets users switch between Agent mode for managing tasks across projects and IDE mode for detailed coding and debugging.

The platform supports desktop, web and mobile access, allowing users to start tasks on a computer and follow their progress or add instructions from a phone. Existing TraeWork users can migrate their chat history, account information and local data through an in-app upgrade. The standalone TraeWork service will shut down on October 23. [TRAE, in Chinese]

item.title: YMTC PC550 Review: A PCIe 5.0 SSD Built for Cool, Compact PCs
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: PCIe 5.0 SSDs are no longer a new category. There are already many drives that can deliver very fast read and write speeds. The harder part is putting that level of performance into a laptop, mini PC, or other compact system without creating new problems with heat and power consumption. In those devices, keeping the […]
item.content:encoded:
PCIe 5.0 SSDs are no longer a new category. There are already many drives that can deliver very fast read and write speeds. The harder part is putting that level of performance into a laptop, mini PC, or other compact system without creating new problems with heat and power consumption. In those devices, keeping the drive cool can matter just as much as achieving a high benchmark score.

The YMTC PC550 is built around that balance. In our testing, it delivered performance above its rated figures in several key benchmarks while keeping its thermal behavior under control during a demanding combined workload. The result is a PCIe 5.0 SSD that is not defined by a single peak number, but by how consistently its performance translates into practical use.

Performance on paper, and beyond

We tested the 1TB version of the PC550. According to YMTC’s official specifications, it is rated for sequential read and write speeds of up to 10,500MB/s and 9,500MB/s, along with random read and write performance of up to 1,300K IOPS. YMTC also lists operating power below 6W and idle power below 3mW.

CrystalDiskMark showed that the PC550 was able to go beyond its official sequential-read rating. It reached 11,712.69MB/s for sequential reads and 9,501.92MB/s for sequential writes. The mixed workload test recorded 11,722.69MB/s read performance and 9,500.92MB/s write performance, while random read and write performance reached 1,403K and 1,789K IOPS respectively.

Rated vs. measured performance

Sequential performance is most relevant when moving large files, loading sizeable game assets or working with other bandwidth-heavy data. Random performance matters more when many small requests are being handled at once, such as during application launches or system activity. The PC550’s results in both areas point to a drive with enough headroom for demanding desktop workloads, rather than one that only performs well in a single sequential test.

Sustained write performance beyond the cache

Peak sequential-write specifications describe short, high-speed transfers. To examine what happens during a longer continuous workload, we used Iometer for a 1TB sequential-write test with 1MB transfers, a queue depth of 8, one worker and 100% write operations.

The resulting curve moves from the initial cache-assisted write range into a lower, stable out-of-cache range. Across the 1TB workload, the PC550 recorded an average write speed of 2,002.69MB/s. This result is more useful for understanding sustained write behavior than a short burst benchmark, especially when the drive is handling a large file transfer or another workload that continues after the fast cache area has been used.

Performance in everyday workloads

The PC550 also performed well in broader storage and application tests. It scored 5,213 in PCMark 10’s Full System Drive Benchmark, with an average bandwidth of 803.70MB/s and average access time of 31 microseconds. In 3DMark’s Storage Benchmark, it achieved a score of 4,963, with average bandwidth of 845.84MB/s and average access time of 36 microseconds.

For a local AI workload, we used Ollama to load the Qwen2.5 7B model. Across three runs, the average model loading time was 2.07 seconds.

That makes the model feel almost instant to launch. The PC550’s PCIe 5.0 read speeds help cut down the wait during cold starts and model switching, keeping storage from becoming the bottleneck in a professional AI workflow. For users who frequently switch models, repeat tests, run local inference, or experiment with RAG pipelines, those shorter waits can directly improve overall efficiency.

We also used Delta Force as a game-loading test. The test starts when the “Start Game” button is clicked in the Black Hawk Down mode and ends when loading is complete and the character-selection screen appears. This is a useful storage scenario because the game needs to bring in a large volume of map and character assets while background game services continue to operate.

The PC550 completed the process in 15.38 seconds. A PCIe 4.0 reference drive on the same platform took 16.72 seconds, giving the PC550 a 1.34-second advantage in this test.

Strong thermal performance under combined load

The game-loading result shows what the PC550 can do in practice. But with PCIe 5.0 SSDs, speed is only one part of the picture. Sustained performance often comes with a noticeable thermal cost: published tests commonly place mainstream Gen5 drives in the 60°C to 70°C range under sustained load, while some earlier high-performance designs can approach 80°C when cooling is limited. Heat has become part of what users expect from Gen5 performance.

To put the PC550 through a more demanding scenario, we ran the system stress test while Delta Force was running in the background. This kept the system, game, and storage active at the same time. The test continued for approximately 30 minutes, with the PC550 installed beneath the motherboard’s stock M.2 heatsink in a room maintained at around 27°C.

After approximately 30 minutes, the PC550 had stayed below 50°C throughout the test. Its main temperature sensors averaged 45°C and peaked at 48°C, while the third sensor averaged 42°C and peaked at 45°C.

That sub-50°C result is particularly significant for compact systems, where cooling capacity is limited and every heat source competes for airflow. The PC550 delivered PCIe 5.0 performance without adding a major thermal burden to the system, suggesting more thermal headroom for the CPU, GPU, and other components during sustained use. Together with YMTC’s below-6W operating-power rating, this gives the PC550 a practical advantage in systems where performance and thermals have to be considered together.

A practical PCIe 5.0 SSD

The PC550’s appeal lies in the balance it strikes. PCIe 5.0 SSDs are often judged by peak benchmark numbers, but in a real system, speed has to work alongside heat, power consumption, and the limits of the platform around it. The PC550 brings the performance needed for demanding file transfers, game assets, and local AI workloads while keeping its thermal behavior manageable under sustained use.

For users building compact PCs, all-in-one systems, or other space-constrained devices, the PC550 offers a straightforward path to PCIe 5.0 performance while keeping heat and cooling demands under control. In that sense, it presents a more usable side of the PCIe 5.0 platform—one that is fast enough for demanding work, but easier to integrate into the system around it.

item.title: ByteDance researchers identify cause of inconsistent long-context retrieval in DeepSeek models
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Researchers from ByteDance’s Seed team have identified a mechanism behind inconsistent long-context retrieval in DeepSeek models. Their study found that chunked KV-cache compression makes retrieval accuracy sensitive to where information falls within a compression window, producing differences of up to 40 percentage points across positions. The technique reduces memory and attention costs by compressing groups […]
item.content:encoded:
Researchers from ByteDance’s Seed team have identified a mechanism behind inconsistent long-context retrieval in DeepSeek models. Their study found that chunked KV-cache compression makes retrieval accuracy sensitive to where information falls within a compression window, producing differences of up to 40 percentage points across positions.

The technique reduces memory and attention costs by compressing groups of consecutive tokens into fewer cache entries. However, the researchers found that the same information can be easy to retrieve at one position and difficult at another, a pattern they call “phase sensitivity.” They reproduced the behavior in models trained from scratch and found that different attention components specialize in retrieving information from different positions. The findings explain how strong average benchmark results can conceal recurring retrieval weaknesses. [ByteDance Seed research paper]

item.title: JD.com’s $2.5 billion Ceconomy takeover moves closer to EU approval
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: JD.com’s proposed $2.5 billion takeover of German electronics retailer Ceconomy is expected to receive European Union approval after the Chinese company revised commitments addressing regulatory concerns, according to a Reuters report cited by IT Home. The European Commission is due to decide on the transaction by November 4. Ceconomy owns the MediaMarkt and Saturn retail […]
item.content:encoded:
JD.com’s proposed $2.5 billion takeover of German electronics retailer Ceconomy is expected to receive European Union approval after the Chinese company revised commitments addressing regulatory concerns, according to a Reuters report cited by IT Home. The European Commission is due to decide on the transaction by November 4.

Ceconomy owns the MediaMarkt and Saturn retail chains. The EU’s review under its Foreign Subsidies Regulation examined whether preferential financing, tax benefits or government support gave JD.com an advantage in the acquisition. JD.com’s revised commitments include providing Ceconomy with European logistics and technology services at market prices and allowing smaller competitors access on fair, non-discriminatory terms. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: Ecosia switches from Mistral to open-weight AI models including Qwen, GLM and Kimi
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: German search engine Ecosia is replacing Mistral with open-weight AI models, including Chinese-developed Qwen, GLM and Kimi, through a partnership with German AI platform Melious. Founder and CEO Christian Kroll said the switch had roughly halved costs while improving quality and performance. Ecosia adopted Mistral in May after moving away from OpenAI, but Kroll said […]
item.content:encoded:
German search engine Ecosia is replacing Mistral with open-weight AI models, including Chinese-developed Qwen, GLM and Kimi, through a partnership with German AI platform Melious. Founder and CEO Christian Kroll said the switch had roughly halved costs while improving quality and performance.

Ecosia adopted Mistral in May after moving away from OpenAI, but Kroll said it encountered recurring technical problems, including overloaded servers, and was disappointed with model quality. The new arrangement gives Ecosia access to multiple models through Melious rather than relying on a single AI developer. [POLITICO]
